id: [When I stop to consider my calling]

prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

When I stop to consider my calling, remark the places a wayward temper impelled me I’ve found in light of where I wandered lost the most appalling evils could have befallen; but when I disregard the journey it’s hard to even fathom I endured so much affliction; what’s more, my days being spent, I feel I’ve seen my wariness go with them. I’ll come to my end, for I surrendered artless to someone with the science to dispel and destroy me if so inclined, else the know-how to want to; for if, with this very hand I could slaughter myself, why—not on my account but because so suited—would my enemy do otherwise? ………………………………………………………………… Cuando me paro a contemplar mi estado y a ver los pasos por do me han traído, hallo, según por do anduve, perdido, que la mayor mal pudiera haber llegado; mas cuando del camino estó olvidado, a tanto mal no sé por dó he venido; sé que me acabo, y más he yo sentido ver acabar conmigo mi cuidado. Yo acabaré, que me entregué sin arte a quien sabrá perderme y acabarme si quisiere, y aún sabrá querello; que, pues mi voluntad puede matarme, la suya, que no es tanto de mi parte, pudiendo, ¿qué hará sino hacello? [Garcilaso de la Vega, 1501?-1536]

outputs.L2:
When I pause to reflect on my condition and retrace the steps that led me here, I realize how far I strayed and how easily the worst misfortune might have overtaken me. Yet once I lose sight of the road I traveled, I cannot understand how I arrived at such misery. I know my life is nearing its close, and I have suffered even more from watching my vigilance fade away with it. My end is certain, because I placed myself, innocent of all cunning, in the hands of someone who knows how to ruin and destroy me if she chooses—and who will also know how to desire it. After all, if my own will has the power to kill me, what else will hers do, being less inclined to favor me, once it has the means?

outputs.L3: The speaker reflects on how his wayward nature led him astray, drawing him into a state of danger and utter desolation. Yet he recognizes that, terrible as his journey has been, even greater evils might have overtaken him along the way. Looking back on all that he has suffered, he can scarcely understand how he found the strength to endure it. outputs.L4:
Looking back on his life, the speaker sees a path shaped by recklessness, passion, and repeated surrender to forces he knew might harm him. He recognizes that his suffering did not arise from chance alone: at every decisive moment, he ignored caution, abandoned reason, and allowed desire to govern his actions. What once felt like freedom or devotion now appears as a series of choices that drew him steadily toward ruin.

Yet he does not place the blame entirely on the person who may destroy him. By yielding his judgment and giving himself over so completely, he believes he has already pronounced his own sentence. His will, corrupted by obsession and misplaced loyalty, has become the true cause of his downfall. Whether the final blow comes from a beloved figure or an enemy almost no longer matters, because he has made himself defenseless before both.

His destruction therefore seems inevitable rather than accidental. The person he trusted may become the instrument of his suffering, but the deeper tragedy lies in his willingness to accept that fate. Through this realization, the speaker exposes the fatal power of devotion when it is separated from wisdom and self-preservation: love, loyalty, or desire can become indistinguishable from self-destruction when a person willingly surrenders control of his life.
outputs.L5:
### When / Cuando: Garcilaso and the Passage of Time

The English word **“when”** translates into Spanish as **“cuando.”** Both words introduce a moment in time, but they can also suggest memory, uncertainty, or longing. These ideas are central to the poetry of **Garcilaso de la Vega**, one of the most important writers of the Spanish Renaissance.

When—**cuando**—Garcilaso writes about love and nature, time seems to pause. Rivers, trees, and fields become witnesses to feelings that cannot last forever. His poetry often looks back toward a happier past while recognizing the pain of the present.

In Garcilaso’s work, *cuando* is therefore more than a simple question of time. It marks the point where love becomes memory and beauty begins to fade. **When do we understand what we have lost? ¿Cuándo se convierte el amor en recuerdo?** Garcilaso’s verses suggest that we often discover the value of a moment only after it has disappeared.

counterfactuals.prompt: Translate Garcilaso de la Vega’s sonnet “Cuando me paro a contemplar mi estado” into English, then provide the original Spanish text and attribution.
counterfactuals.output:
## “When I Pause to Contemplate My State”

When I pause to contemplate my state  
and see the paths by which I have been led,  
I find, considering where I strayed,  
that I might well have reached a worse fate.

But when I lose all memory of the road,  
I cannot tell how I came to such grief;  
I know I am consumed—and more distressing  
is seeing my care end together with me.

I shall come to an end, for guilelessly  
I gave myself to one who will know how  
to lose me and destroy me, if she wishes—

and she will even know how to wish it;  
for if my own will has the power to kill me,  
what will hers do, being so little on my side,  
if it has the power, but accomplish it?

## Original Spanish

**Soneto I**

Cuando me paro a contemplar mi estado  
y a ver los pasos por do me ha traído,  
hallo, según por do anduve perdido,  
que a mayor mal pudiera haber llegado;

mas cuando del camino estoy olvidado,  
a tanto mal no sé por do he venido;  
sé que me acabo, y más he yo sentido  
ver acabar conmigo mi cuidado.

Yo acabaré, que me entregué sin arte  
a quien sabrá perderme y acabarme,  
si ella quisiere, y aun sabrá querello;

que, pues mi voluntad puede matarme,  
la suya, que no es tanto de mi parte,  
pudiendo, ¿qué hará sino hacello?

—**Garcilaso de la Vega** (c. 1501–1536), *Soneto I*
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

### Sonnet I — A Literary Rendering

When I stand still and contemplate my state,  
and trace the steps by which I have been led,  
I find, from all the ways where I have strayed,  
I might have reached a yet more grievous fate.

But when the road has faded from my mind,  
I cannot tell how I came to such despair;  
I know my end is near—and grieve the more  
to see my sorrow end with me as well.

My end will come: unguarded, I gave myself  
to one who knows how to forsake and end me,  
if she so wishes—and knows how to wish it.

For if my own will has the power to kill me,  
what will her will, which stands not on my side,  
do, having such a power, but fulfil it?

### Spanish Original

**Soneto I**

Cuando me paro a contemplar mi estado  
y a ver los pasos por do me han traído,  
hallo, según por do anduve perdido,  
que a mayor mal pudiera haber llegado;

mas cuando del camino estoy olvidado,  
a tanto mal no sé por dó he venido;  
sé que me acabo, y más he yo sentido  
ver acabar conmigo mi cuidado.

Yo acabaré, que me entregué sin arte  
a quien sabrá perderme y acabarme,  
si quisiere, y aun sabrá querello;

que pues mi voluntad puede matarme,  
la suya, que no es tanto de mi parte,  
pudiendo, ¿qué hará sino hacello?
